Chapter Fourteen: The Combined Chapters (End of Part Seven).
As for why this chapter has come to be included, it possesses six meanings. First, the Master of the Treatise [has] clearly explained above...
All phenomena are without dependence and without cessation.
Outsiders believe this and say:
"If one says there is dependence and cessation," [it would contradict their view].
One must not respond to the Prajñāpāramitā by conceptualizing the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Now, if one can be without dependence and without interruption,
such that both emptiness and existence are equally pure, only then does one attain union with the true mark.
Therefore, I shall now further refute this to clarify that since there is neither dependence nor severance, how could there be joining or dispersal?
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"When a bodhisattva practices prajñā..."
Not perceiving either conjunction or non-conjunction, nor perceiving what is appropriate or inappropriate—
this is what is called being in correspondence with *prajñā*.
The masters of the *Saṃgraha* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) posit that the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha is in correspondence with the *dharmakāya*, yet they too are subject to this same critique.
Second, the four kinds of attachments mentioned above all arise from the mind forming conceptual understandings;
therefore, these attachments are refuted.
Consequently, in this chapter, one further investigates and examines phenomena, body and mind, as well as the person and self, finding that ultimately none of them can be apprehended.
Who creates this understanding?
Furthermore, by what means does attachment arise?
Thirdly, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are called the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Although the meaning of the emptiness of the five aggregates has been examined in the "Chapter on the Five Aggregates," it is not yet exhaustive;
therefore, one should further examine and investigate them from the perspective of the practice of the gates [of the senses].
In terms of their essential nature, they consist solely of the six sense faculties.
Although the preceding "Chapter on the Six Faculties" contemplates that the six faculties are unobtainable, its meaning is not yet exhaustive.
This chapter exists because one further investigates and examines their union with the sense objects, finding that it has no source.
Thus, this chapter was composed.
Fourth, the Chapter on Practice refutes the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Now, it refutes the conjunction of conditions between the sense faculties (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya); therefore, its substantial existence has already been refuted above.
Now, this provisional existence is refuted.
Question: For what reason does one contemplate that the six sense organs do not unite with the six sense objects?
Answer: Deluded sentient beings perceive the organs and objects as two distinct entities.
Thus, when the sense faculties and their objects come together, the afflictions of the three poisons arise.
Because of these afflictions, there is karma; because of karma, there is the fruit of suffering.
Now, observing that the faculties and their objects are fundamentally without conjunction,
afflictions do not arise; thus,
there is neither karma nor suffering.
Fifth, although the "Chapter on Superior Practice" refutes the doctrine of difference,
it does so only briefly and the meaning remains not yet fully exhausted;
in this present chapter, all doctrines of the difference of dharmas are extensively refuted.
The reason for refuting difference is that conjunction arises from difference;
since there is no difference, there is no conjunction.
Therefore, it refutes difference.
Sixth, all streams of sentient beings regard the myriad phenomena as distinct;
arising from the obstacle of delusion, they fail to attain liberation.
Now, in this chapter, since no basis can be found for the notion that all phenomena are distinct, afflictions do not arise;
therefore, this chapter asks: "Who conceives of conjunction?"
The answer is that there are briefly four masters.
First, worldly people commonly say that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) combine with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
Second, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that consciousness arises from the conjunction of the spirit, the mind, and the sense objects.
The Abhidharmikas say that there exists a separate category of "contact" (sparśa) capable of bringing together the sense faculties and their objects.
The Sarvāstivādins clarify that the sense faculty and the object simply conjoin, and there is no separate category of contact.
Now, as no further meaning can be sought to harmonize with this,
the chapter is thus titled "The Chapter on the Eye" (*cakṣu-varga*). This chapter is divided into two sections.
First, the introduction by prose;
second, the main body of the verses which correctly refutes [the opponent] without conjunction.
The first [section] further has two parts.
The purpose of the preceding "Chapter on Origination" has been explained;
next, the reason for the lack of synthesis is questioned.
This chapter is titled "The Proponent" (Vādī).
Exchanging words is called "discourse" (*lun*);
speaking directly is termed "exposition" (*shuo*).
Since this chapter extensively analyzes and discriminates the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is titled accordingly.
It is not that the externalist merely follows up on a previous question;
therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, the superior grade proceeds from the investigation of the real and the unreal, culminating in the refutation of the layered emptiness."
The opponents’ mouths and eyes cannot save them, for their minds have not yet awakened.
The Master, anticipating their mental state, seizes it and refutes it;
thus it is said that the eight verses are divided into three parts.
The first two verses grant the possibility of difference while refuting the possibility of union.
The second five verses directly refute the absence of difference.
The third single verse clarifies that because there is no difference, there is no union.
The first [section] also has two parts.
The preceding verse clarifies that because the three factors—seeing and so forth—are distinct, there is no conjunction.
The second verse clarifies that because all phenomena are distinct, there is no conjunction.
Because the three factors are distinct, there is no conjunction.
The eye and the form are dharmas;
the seer is a person.
Since the person and the dharmas are distinct, how could they be conjoined?
Within the category of dharmas, visible form constitutes the external and the eye constitutes the internal;
since the internal and external are distinct, there is likewise no conjunction.
Question: Regarding the world, the non-Buddhists, the Mahāyāna, and the Hīnayāna, they only clarify that the eye and form are distinct yet conjoined.
"Conjoined" means that the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) meet; thus, it is said they are "conjoined.
Now, however, you say they are "distinct and not conjoined. How is this so?
This appears to be precisely the meaning of the "external" (bāhya);
why then is it called "refutation" (prabheda)?
The answer is that this has two meanings.
First, because the essence of the sense organ and the object are distinct, there is no principle of reaching [the object] through form;
therefore, there is no conjunction. If one were to claim that they conjoin from a distance, then since they do not reach it, they would likewise fail to conjoin with a nearby color.
Furthermore, that which does not reach the distant cannot be conjoined with the distant.
Herein, the refutation of difference establishes that conjunction is impossible;
for the Sautrāntikas, the conventional person cannot be conjoined with the real [person], as they are distinct.
The mind and the true reality differ from the stubborn realm (the phenomenal world), and thus they cannot be conjoined.
The masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* should likewise realize that the physical body is impermanent and differs from the Dharma-body, and thus they cannot be conjoined.
This long passage consists of five parts.
First, to explain the root verse:
"Whether I am within or without" means that practitioners of the Buddha-dharma conceive of the self as being inside the body.
Just as a tree spirit relies upon the tree and has no other distinct location.
Furthermore, the second section below opens two points of inquiry to interrogate [the opponent].
The reason for opening these two points of inquiry to interrogate is as follows:
The above clarifies that because the three factors are distinct, there is no conjunction.
The opponent does not accept this objection;
[they argue] that if the three factors were not distinct, then there would indeed be no conjunction.
Precisely because these three matters are distinct, there must be a conjunction;
therefore, he again opens two points of inquiry to challenge this.
Furthermore, these inquiries amount to five.
First, the citation; second, the determination; third, the general negation; fourth, the formal objection; fifth, the summary conclusion.
The text is easy to understand. Question:
You claim that the eye must reach the object in order to see fire.
If one were to see fire, it should burn the eyes;
furthermore, one should be able to see the fish and stones within a deep pool,
and the eyes should be soaked by the water.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya school claims that the eye possesses cognition through contact with an object external to itself.
Why must it necessarily be so for others?
For example, fish and other such creatures perceive at night without depending on light.
Furthermore, when a Mahāsattva enters meditative absorption through the faculty of the eye and arises from samādhi through the ear,
what fixed rule governs their separation or conjunction?
Furthermore, those who uphold the Lotus Sūtra can smell fragrances from afar.
Why must the three sense organs necessarily reach their objects before they perceive them?
Moreover, according to your claim that "joining from afar" implies "reaching from afar," [the organ] would have to arrive at the distant object.
It cannot be reached from afar, nor can it be heard from afar.
Furthermore, regarding the Sāṃkhya claim that the six consciousnesses cognize the six objects:
if you hold that there is only one consciousness for the six sense organs, then a single organ would possess all six functions.
The six sense organs and the six consciousnesses function simultaneously.
Question: Thirdly, the opponent defends his position by clarifying that cognition arises from the conjunction of four factors.
Since cognition has already arisen, this serves as proof for the conjunction of the self, the object, the sense organ, and the attention.
Therefore, the result is cited to prove the cause.
The response is divided into two parts: first, the refutation of the defense in the fourth section below;
second, the analysis according to the text.
The first point refers back to the previous refutation.
In the "Chapter on the Six Sense Faculties," it was clarified that among the three factors, vision does not exist:
first, the eye itself cannot see.
Two forms cannot see each other;
three persons cannot see [a single form].
Because there is no seeing, there is no conjunction.
Since there is no conjunction, cognition does not arise;
therefore, it is said that the four dharmas, beginning with consciousness, do not exist.
This fully refutes both cause and effect.
How can one further use the effect to prove the cause?
Moreover, in the "Chapter on the Faculties" (Indriya-varga), it was stated that there is no seeing, no seer, and no visible objects.
Now, one should not say that cognition arises through the conjunction of these four.
Now, I shall further explain the second section, the "Refutation by Granting the Opponent's Position," which is divided into five parts.
First, the restatement of the opponent's argument.
Next, the external arguments are restated;
next, two critical points are opened to resolve them;
and fourth, an objection is raised.
"Knowing there is no [inherent] cause" concludes the fifth section below.
"Thus, among all these dharmas, like an illusion" below is the fifth prose passage, which provides an analogy to clarify this.
"Defilement and that which is defiled" is the second verse, which clarifies that the myriad dharmas are distinct; therefore, there is no conjunction.
The first half clarifies that the three factors, such as defilement and so forth,
lack conjunction. The reason for specifically refuting the conjunction of defilement and so forth is that greed arises because the eye sees forms.
It was previously explained that even when the eye sees a form, there is no actual contact;
from what, then, could craving arise?
Therefore, the next section refutes defilement.
Furthermore, as clarified above, if there is no conjunction between the eye and form, then the five sense-faculties lack the principle of conjunction.
Now, if there is no conjunction with passion and so forth, then the mental faculty lacks the principle of conjunction.
The second half of the verse further refutes these two factors by analogy.
The "remaining bases" (*āyatana*) refer to the five bases beginning with the ear.
The "remaining afflictions" refer to the categories of hatred and delusion.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that distinct phenomena must necessarily combine, this second point refutes the notion of their being non-distinct.
Previously, the refutation of difference was established by means of identity; therefore, we shall now distinguish the absence of difference.
Furthermore, conjunction arises from difference, taking difference as its basis.
Since there is currently no difference,
with what could it be conjoined?
Furthermore, it is like the case of the superior grade.
In the preceding superior exposition, [the opponent] used difference to refute identity;
subsequently, they reverted to grasping difference as a defense for identity.
Now, by means of difference, it is shown that [identity] is not established.
The opponent returns to maintain the defense of difference by means of conjunction;
therefore, both chapters contain refutations of difference,
with five verses divided into two parts.
The first two verses provide a general indication of non-differentiation;
the second three verses provide a detailed explanation of non-differentiation. The former [the first two verses] is further divided into two parts.
The preceding verse clarifies that the three dharmas are non-different,
thereby countering the aforementioned [view] that the three dharmas do not conjoin.
The second verse clarifies that all dharmas are non-different.
Regarding all phenomena, there is no conjunction;
this text is easy to understand.
Question: For what reason is it proclaimed that the myriad phenomena are without distinction?
Answer: The worldlings, non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and Mahāyānists all state that the eye and forms are distinct;
therefore, when the eye sees forms, the three poisons and the suffering of karma arise.
Now, if one seeks their distinction and cannot find it, then the three poisons will not arise.
This is of great benefit. Question:
For what reason is there no difference [between this and] the arising of the second and third verses?
These three verses herein are very easy to understand.
However, as commentators have frequently offered divergent interpretations, they have ultimately obscured the text.
Now, I shall read it directly so that it may be clearly and easily understood.
The following three verses are divided into two parts.
The first two verses clarify that there is no difference in the "folding" (the whole).
The subsequent verse distinguishes that there is no difference in the "fingers" (the parts).
Clarifying that there is no difference in the folding means clarifying that there is no difference in the aggregate.
To discern that there is no distinction in the absence of a referent is itself the absence of differentiation.
Now, when discussing distinctions, they do not exceed the categories of the general and the particular.
If there were no difference between the general and the particular, then all distinctions would be empty.
Furthermore, there is no distinct illumination apart from the rolled-up state, which means there is no fruit;
next, there is no distinct illumination apart from the pointing finger, which means there is no cause.
Thus, cause and fruit encompass all phenomena.
Furthermore, the absence of difference in "unfolding" clarifies that there is no difference as conceived by those within our own school;
next, the absence of difference in "pointing" clarifies that there is no difference as conceived by non-Buddhists.
This collectively encompasses all things, both internal and external.
Furthermore, the preceding [section] also clarifies the difference of being without causes and conditions;
next, it clarifies the difference of not being non-causes and conditions,
which likewise encompasses all [phenomena].
To summarize the established meaning:
it was previously clarified that there is no provisional difference,
namely between a provisional person and a provisional pillar.
Next, the lack of substantial difference is explained:
namely, the five aggregates (skandhas) and the four subtle elements (paramāṇus).
By means of the categories of the provisional and the real, all things are subsumed.
The first two verses are further divided into two parts.
The first verse clarifies that the rolled-up state is not different from the fingers;
that is to say, the effect is not different from the cause.
This, too, is a designation that does not differ from reality.
The second verse clarifies that the rolled-up state does not differ from the jar, the pillar, and so forth;
it is likewise that the effect does not differ from what is not its cause.
Now, when discussing distinctions, they do not go beyond these two.
Since these two do not exist, the principle of distinction is exhausted.
As for those who claim that distinction exists because there are things to be distinguished:
"Different" refers to the difference in the act of curling.
"Due to difference" means due to the difference among the five fingers.
"There is difference" means there is the difference in the act of curling.
The reason for this is that when one sees the finger pointing, one knows the five [fingers] as a single roll;
when one sees the fingers spread, one knows the roll as being joined.
Seeing the finger is the cause, and knowing the curling [of the hand] is the effect;

therefore it is said that different causes have different existences. As for the phrase "different words, different non-existences": [it means that] if the words were not different, there would be no difference [in their referents].
"Different" refers to the difference of the curling.
"Separated from difference" means being separated from the difference of the five fingers.
"Without difference" means there is no difference of the curling.
If a phenomenon were not different from its cause,
the first half [of the verse] would establish the position that cause and effect are identical for the opponent;
now, the second half refutes this.
If the effect arises from a cause, then the effect is not different from the cause.
This is because if the cause were destroyed while the effect remained, only then could the effect be different from the cause.
Now, because the effect exists when the cause exists and the effect does not exist when the cause does not exist,
how could one possibly roll the effect back into the cause?
This being so, it is likewise with rolling the finger back into the hand.
People look upon the five aggregates as pillars and the four atoms as the myriad phenomena; all meanings are of this same category.
Question: Above it was clarified that the three dharmas, such as the eye, are without distinction.
May one now likewise take these three dharmas, such as the eye, and employ them as examples?
Answer: It can possess both meanings.
If one considers it from the perspective of its actual formation, the eye is the effect and the four great elements are the cause.
The same applies to the breaking of a finger joint.
According to the Abhidharma,
the eye is also a fruit produced by the four great elements.
This is also a reason:
although it is neither conventional nor substantial, since it is both cause and effect,
it is likewise like the rolled finger.
Second, the eye differs in relation to forms;
because forms differ, there is a difference in the eye.
Apart from the difference in forms, there is no difference in the eye.
If the eye were different from that which arises from form,
then that which arises from form would not be different from the eye;
for the eye is the seer and form is the seen.
Since there is neither that which is seen nor that which is able to see,
the phenomena of subject and object both exist together when they exist, and both are absent when they are absent.
One cannot say that although the object seen is non-existent, the subject that sees still exists.
Therefore, that which destroys is identical to what is destroyed;
one should know that the agent is not different from the object.
Furthermore, it was asked: "The eye and form have never been united from the very beginning."
How can it be said that they are different?
Furthermore, it was asked: "Is the eye different from its cause, and is form different from its cause; and is form different from the eye, and is the eye different from form?
If they were all mutually different, then everything would be both the eye and form.
His answer is based precisely on the fact that the eye is distinct from form and form is distinct from the eye; thus, there is both eye and form.
Why do you raise this objection? You ask:
"Is it because the eye is distinct that it serves as the cause for the production of a distinct form?"
It is because they do not arise from a different cause.
If they were to arise from a different cause,
then difference would depend upon difference, and length would depend upon length.
If the cause does not differ from that which arises,
then since you refer to both the eye and the form,
how can they not be different?
He asked again: "Does this 'otherness' have a distinct entity, or does it lack a distinct entity?
If otherness lacks a distinct entity, then it must refer back to form (rūpa) itself as its entity."
Furthermore, since the eye has no separate essence, it refers back to visible form as its very essence.
If the eye were to take the eye itself as its essence rather than taking visible form as its essence, [it would be untenable].
Furthermore, difference itself takes difference as its essence;
it does not take form (rūpa) as its essence.
Moreover, only if form possessed an essence could it be designated as "difference."
Since form ultimately has no essence,
how could there be difference?
Furthermore, difference is designated as having form as its essence.
Furthermore, by what does form have its essence?
If that essence itself had an essence, there would be an infinite regress; and if there were an infinite regress, there would be no essence at all.
Furthermore, difference does not have form as its essence;
rather, form itself is difference.
Thus, when one perceives form, one should perceive difference.
If this [object] is distinct from the mental object-field (dharmāyatana), how can the eye see it?
If it does not see it, then form is not something distinct.
There should be a distinct difference from form;
that difference should possess its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, regarding this difference existing in the eye, does it reside in the eye itself or in the form?
If it resides in the eye, from what does the difference in the eye arise?
If it resides in the form, this is a difference in the form;
how does it concern a difference in the eye?
Furthermore, if the eye were different from itself yet not different [from others], it would be both one and not one.
Just as it is one with respect to a jar,
it would likewise be one with respect to a jar but not one with respect to a pillar.
Then the eye would be distinct and yet distinct from the eye;
how could it exist within form?
Furthermore, this refutes the notion that a phenomenon arises from its own cause.
Just as fire arises from wood,
yet the fire cannot return to the wood;
if the fire were to return to the wood and emerge from it once again, [it would be impossible].
If fire likewise returns to water, why does it not emerge from water?
Just as a house is established by means of pillars but not by means of space,
we know that space is distinct from the house, whereas the pillars are not distinct from the house.
If they were both different, they would both be established as such.
Furthermore, one should apply this refutation to all distinctions, such as those between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, or ordinary beings and sages;
for instance, because there is the distinction of nirvāṇa, there is the distinction of saṃsāra.
There is no difference between nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, nor is there any difference between the real and the false; it is the same for all such pairs.
Question: If there were a definitively distinct dharma, what fault would there be? The second verse refutes the notion that the fruit is not distinct from what is not its cause.
The question was asked first and the answer followed.
The opponent said:
"Rolling up exists because of the fingers."
The coiling is not different from the finger;
yet the coiling does not exist by virtue of the pillar.
Therefore, the coiling should be distinct from the pillar.
Therefore, it is called the "dharma of fixed distinction.
In the response, the first half [of the verse] concedes [the opponent's position], while the second half refutes it.
As for what is meant by "conceding":
If there were a distinct "folding" apart from the five fingers,
then that folding could be considered distinct from things such as a jar or a pillar. This concludes the refutation of the latter half [of the opponent's position].
Now, since there is no distinctness apart from the five fingers, and likewise no distinctness in the state of being curled, by what thing could there be distinctness from the jar or the pillar?
In this manner, one should apply this refutation to all things: that the five aggregates constitute a person and the four atoms constitute a pillar.
The prose commentary provides two cycles of explanation:
the first explains by way of a general treatment of all phenomena;
the second explains by way of specific references to particular matters.
Question: My scripture explains that the second [level of] descent breaks the five fingers individually.
This is fully detailed as previously enumerated in the items.
First the question, then the answer.
The intent of the question is twofold:
first, to present generally what it is;
second, to explain specifically what it is.
The statement that "distinct characteristics do not arise from multiple conditions" generally summarizes what has been established.
The preceding two verses both concern the principle of arising from causes and conditions.
In the first verse, the scroll exists by virtue of the fingers; the scroll is not distinct from the fingers.
The next verse states: "A rolled-up mat exists from its constituent parts, yet when unrolled it is non-existent; thus, it could be different from a jar.
However, since both arise from causes and conditions, there is no difference between them.
Now, the outsider says:
In my sūtras, I have taught that distinct characteristics do not arise from causes and conditions;
this must therefore involve a fixed, distinct dharma.
This is the unsurpassed refutation.
Regarding the "general characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) discussed below, this is the second section, which specifically identifies what they are.
The general characteristic is the rolled-up state;
the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are the individual features such as the length of the five fingers.
"Different dharmas" refers to the five fingers as entities.
Because they are distinguished by being collectively curled, there is the differentiation of the length and shortness of the five fingers.
Due to these differing characteristics of length and shortness among the fingers, there exists the dharma of the five fingers.
This is because one knows the length or shortness of a finger by means of the finger itself;
therefore, the length or shortness of the finger is used as its distinguishing characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
"Length" and "shortness" are names for distinct dharmas.

Question: Since the opponent has already stated that there are particular characteristics derived from general characteristics, and distinct phenomena derived from dissimilar characteristics, how can it be said that they do not arise from causes and conditions?
Answer: The author will provide this refutation below.
However, the opponent's position states that from the five fingers, the fist arises as a distinct whole; therefore,
the whole is produced from causes and conditions.
This is because when the individual fingers are destroyed, the collective fist is also destroyed;
the individual fingers do not arise from the collective fist.
Since the fingers still persist even though the fist is destroyed, we know that the individual characteristics are not produced from the collective characteristic.
Thus we know that particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) constitute the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, we know that particular characteristics do not arise from causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya).
This principle is largely identical to the doctrines concerning the provisional and the real found in the *Tattvasiddhi* and other texts.
The person is established from the subtle aggregates;
when the subtle aggregates perish, the person perishes.
The subtle aggregates are not established from the person.
Although the person-pillar (pudgala-stambha) is destroyed, it still possesses the four subtle elements (mahābhūta) and the five aggregates (skandha).
The first half of the verse refutes the absence of distinct characteristics;
the second half clarifies the absence of distinct dharmas. The first half opens two gates to interrogate [the opponent].
You take the length and shortness of the fingers as the distinguishing characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since the long and short fingers are the distinct phenomena (*dharma*),
you thus take the length and shortness of the fingers as the characteristic of the "long and short fingers."
Is it that the long and short fingers are fundamentally different, and thus characterized by different characteristics?
Or is it that the long and short fingers are fundamentally not different, yet characterized by different characteristics?
If the long and short fingers were fundamentally different...
In the end, why is it necessary for a characteristic of difference to characterize them?
Furthermore, if they were inherently different and yet required a further characteristic of difference to characterize them,
there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (redundant difference).
Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress.
If the long and short fingers were fundamentally not different, yet you claim they are characterized by difference,
this too is not tenable.
If the two fingers were originally not distinct, then there would be no characteristic of duality;
what, then, would be characterized?
Furthermore, you use the characteristic of difference to characterize that which is non-different, thereby making it different.

Furthermore, by means of the principle that "non-difference" is not different from "you," the characteristic of difference should also establish non-difference through the characteristic of difference.
Again, it is asked: Is your "difference" different from difference?
Or is it different yet non-different?
If they were different,
then since they are already different, what need is there for further difference?
If they were not different, then...
Then there would be no further non-difference. How could there be difference?
It is like fire being hot.
Regarding heat, it is either hot or not hot.
If heat is already hot, then since it is already heated, what further need is there for it to be heated?
If there were neither heat nor non-heat,
then there would be no non-heat; how, then, could there be heat?
The second half states:

"Because there are distinct characteristics of length and shortness, there are these distinct phenomena of 'this' and 'that' fingers; since such distinct characteristics do not exist [in this case], [there is no such distinction]."
How can there be such distinct phenomena as "this" and "that"?
This long passage is divided into two parts;
the first is a preliminary refutation of the thesis established by the opponent.
Next, the verse is explained.
The initial section has two parts:
first, restating the opponent's position.
If that is so, the following is the second refutation:
Since it has already been stated that because one discriminates the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), there exists a particular characteristic (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa),
one should know that the particular characteristic arises from the perception of the general.
How can it be said that distinct characteristics do not arise from conditions?

The proponents of the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury) say: "One must first discuss the fundamental existence of matter and mind, and only then discourse upon their general and particular aspects."
It is like having two pillars standing in the middle and only then discussing their east and west.
Now I ask you: is the distinct [part] distinct from the distinct, or is it distinct from the whole?
If they are distinct from one another,
then being already distinct,
what further need is there for them to be distinct?
If the particular and the universal were distinct, then the particular would arise from the universal;
furthermore, since the particular is distinct from the universal, the universal would be lost.
The same applies to the whole as well.

Regarding the statement that "a distinct characteristic cannot be found apart from the distinct phenomena," this clarifies that because the particular arises from the general, the particular constitutes the meaning of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Now, it is explained that the characteristic of difference arises from a different dharma; this is the meaning of "conditioned origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
For example, length and shortness must arise from fingers that are long and short.
Therefore, the characteristic of difference is itself conditioned origination.
Therefore, all things are merely causes and conditions.
If they were such causes and conditions, they would have already been refuted by the preceding two verses.
Now, following the principle that "within distinct phenomena there is no distinct characteristic," the second verse of the original text is explained.
The meaning is easy to see.
If a distinct characteristic were present within a non-distinct phenomenon but was not called a "non-distinct phenomenon," this would contradict the intended meaning,
as it is not permitted for the distinct to exist within the non-distinct.
If the characteristic of difference were present within non-difference, then there would be no such thing as the dharma of non-difference.
Since even the dharma of non-difference does not exist,
how can you say that the characteristic of difference exists within non-difference?
This point must be understood by reversing it.
Furthermore, the third section below explains that because there is no difference, there is no conjunction;
this is precisely the interpretation of the preceding refutation of difference.
The chapter is titled "Refuting Conjunction" (Póhé),
yet here we refute "difference" (yì);
the intention is to clarify that there is no conjunction.
The first half further opens two gates—identity and difference—to clarify the absence of conjunction;
the second half concludes the meaning of the absence of conjunction.
There is no conjunction because there are three inherent meanings [of non-conjunction].
If that which is capable of uniting is itself without anything to unite with,
then that which is united lacks the capacity to unite.
Were it otherwise, it would not be the relationship of agent and object.
There is no conjunction.
That which is a different dharma does not conjoin;
for if it is different, it is already established as such.
There is no need for further conjunction;
even if there were conjunction, it would still be untenable.
For example, when one side of a finger is joined, the other three sides are not joined.
Because "non-conjunction" is manifold, it should be combined to form "conjunction.
Chapter Fifteen: On Existence and Non-existence (End of Section Seven). Regarding this chapter, there are two meanings concerning its proximity and distance.
In the preceding chapters, the existence and non-existence [of things] have been refuted in various places. It is said:
"If there were no 'existence' (bhāva)..."
How could there be non-existence?
As it says in the Chapter on Formations (Saṃskāra-varga):
"If there were non-empty phenomena, there would have to be empty phenomena."
Thus, these have all been refuted.
What has preceded was a brief refutation by way of analysis;
what follows is a detailed refutation by way of synthesis.
The reason one must compose both extensive and abbreviated refutations is that existence and non-existence are the roots of all views and obstacles to the Middle Way. As for the roots of these views,
they establish the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism based on existence and non-existence.
Because the views of sixty-two types arise from clinging to existence and non-existence,
existence and non-existence are the root of all these views.
If the disease of existence and non-existence arises, then all manner of diseases arise together.
If existence and non-existence are extinguished, all afflictions are extinguished.
Regarding that which obstructs the fundamental Middle Way,
speaking in terms of what is proximate:
All causes and effects are the Middle Way.
Furthermore, Buddha-nature is the Middle Way,
as when the Buddha rebuked Kāśyapa.
I did not previously state that the Middle Way is the Buddha-nature;
why have you lost your way of understanding and asked again?
Furthermore, the Middle Way is the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
In this way, the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle is entirely the Middle Way.
Now, the arising of existence and non-existence constitutes the faults of nihilism and eternalism, thereby obstructing the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata always relies upon the two truths (*satyadvaya*) when teaching the Dharma.
The two truths are merely emptiness and existence as dependent origination;
yet when outsiders hear of "existence," they understand it as the existence of intrinsic nature,
and when they hear of "non-existence," they understand it as the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
This would obstruct the two truths;
once the two truths are obstructed, the two wisdoms do not arise, and consequently,
there would be no Buddhas or Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
Since this illness is so deep-seated, it must be thoroughly refuted.
Furthermore, as for those who have come with this chapter, some say:
This treatise, from beginning to end, refutes and washes away all dharmas;
it is essentially a dismantling of existence to enter non-existence, and a dismissal of the conventional to return to the ultimate truth.
Now, I say this is not so.
Since one seeks both existence and non-existence from them,
what is there to dismantle?
Upon examination, neither is found.
What is it that enters?
It is simply that the deluded cling to existence, while those who mislead others claim non-existence;
now, when examined, neither can be established.
Therefore, it is said that existence and non-existence are refuted.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Creator" states:
"This karma arises from a multitude of conditions."
Existence and non-existence are merely provisional designations and lack any definitive reality;
they are not as you have described.

Therefore, it should be known that the externalist has nothing to perceive regarding existence, nor does he have anything to perceive regarding non-existence, up to and including the five propositions.
Therefore, one should know that this existence and non-existence are not subsumed within the two truths.
It cannot be said that this treatise negates existence in order to enter into non-existence,
for it lacks those perceived [notions of] existence and non-existence.

Only then can one understand that the provisional designations of existence and non-existence arising from causes and conditions have no beginning; this is the Buddha’s two truths, the ultimate and the conventional.
Furthermore, for practitioners of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, hearing of existence and non-existence is the root of various views that constitute obstacles to the Path.
One then seeks to extinguish the two views of existence and non-existence;
now, in order to destroy this person's illness, it is clarified that existence and non-existence are fundamentally unarisen—what, then, is there to be extinguished?
As for your statement that "existence exists and non-existence exists":
If one seeks it, it should be obtainable;
since it cannot be obtained through seeking, how can there be "existence" or "non-existence"?

Furthermore, all those who practice the Way, practice seated meditation, or study the teachings, who say that there is a Way to be sought, dhyāna to be practiced, or principles to be learned—all such views are the view of existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The absence of what is not the Way, up to and including the absence of what is not the ultimate meaning, is itself non-view.
Even if one says that there has never been such a thing as "non-existence," in the end there remains the Way of neither existence nor non-existence.
There is still the view of existence.
If there were no such path that is neither existent nor non-existent, it would be the view of non-existence.
Therefore, the maladies of existence and non-existence are difficult to abandon.
For this reason, the Master of Treatises diligently refutes it in various chapters.
Next, in the chapter refuting conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he clarifies the refutation of existence and non-existence.
An ignorant person says:
When various conditions combine, all phenomena come into being;
when those conditions disperse, the myriad transformations cease to exist.
Since there is both existence and non-existence, how could there be a combination?
Furthermore, there is no difference between the superior [type of] refutation and [the opponent's position]. The opponent says:
"There is no 'non-difference' characteristic; rather, there is a dharma that possesses difference."
Since existence and non-existence both exist, how can they not be different?
Furthermore, existence differs from non-existence, and non-existence differs from existence.
Since both existence and non-existence exist, there is indeed a difference between them.
Furthermore, an external opponent challenges the proponent:
"If you say there is no difference [between existence and non-existence], then the two truths should not exist.
Since the two truths do indeed exist, there must be a difference between existence and non-existence."
Question: What is meant by existence and non-existence?
Answer: There are many approaches to existence and non-existence.
If explained in terms of cause and effect:
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the effect exists within the cause;
the Vaiśeṣikas hold that the effect does not exist within the cause;
and the Lokāyatas maintain that the effect both exists and does not exist within the cause.
This is both existent and non-existent.
Within the Buddha-dharma, the Sarvāstivāda school clarifies that the three periods of time exist;
they designate this as "existence."
According to the second generation of the Dharmaguptaka school, that which lacks a name is termed "non-existent.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains the Sarvāstivāda tenets as follows:
when a cause is produced in the present, it exists in the future.
If one does not act as a cause in the present, it will not exist in the future;
therefore, the future both exists and does not exist.
According to the doctrine of the Kāśyapīyas, once it has acted as a cause, it immediately passes away into the past.
It is designated as "existent" [at the time it arises],
and only upon the completion of its arising in dependence upon a fruit does it cease and become non-existent;
this is what is meant by the past being both existent and non-existent.
If one examines the existence or non-existence of persons and dharmas,
the three types of non-Buddhists all reckon that persons and dharmas exist;
this they designate as "existence."
The heterodox practitioners of wrong views deny the existence of persons and phenomena,
labeling them as non-existent;
Kālakauṭa, however, gives rise to views based on the objects before him.
If someone asks whether it exists, one answers that it exists;
if someone asks whether it does not exist, one immediately answers that it does not exist.
This is called "both existing and non-existing."
Within the Buddha-dharma there are also three schools.
The Vātsīputrīyas maintain that both persons and dharmas exist;
they designate this as "existence."
The Vaipulya school calculates that there is neither person nor dharma,
naming this "non-existence" (Sarvāstivāda); the Sarvāstivāda school holds that there is no person but there are dharmas,
which they designate as "both existence and non-existence."
If one discusses existence and non-existence in terms of objects and consciousness,
the traditional Mahāyāna teachings clarify that both objects and consciousness exist;
whereas the Fangguang (Vaipulya) teachings clarify that neither objects nor consciousness exist.
If the mind has no object, there would be the dust [the external realm] but no consciousness;
if it is the theory of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), then there is no dust but only consciousness.
Question: For what causes and conditions do sentient beings give rise to views of existence and non-existence?
The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) answers:
"Those with an abundance of craving cling to existence;
those with an abundance of views cling to non-existence."
All sentient beings possess only craving and views.
As clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they are like venomous insects and malevolent spirits.
Furthermore, those with an abundance of the four views are attached to existence.
Those with many wrong views are attached to non-existence.
Now it is clarified that such [views] are all coarse theories concerning existence and non-existence.
A student of the Mahāyāna should precisely recognize the subtle marks of obstruction in a bodhisattva.
If the mind arises with the notion of existence, it is called "existence";
as soon as the mind arises with the notion of non-existence, it is called "non-existence.
Now, because such notions of existence and non-existence have been stilled, it is said that "the chapter on destroying existence and non-existence" has been concluded.
The chapter is divided into two parts:
first, refuting the existence and non-existence separately;
second, refuting the existence and non-existence collectively.
There are four [points] each for separation and conjunction.
Regarding the four points of separation,
the first is the refutation of intrinsic existence.
Next, the existence of others is refuted;
third, the external existence of both self and others is refuted;
fourth, non-existence is refuted.
Regarding the initial refutation of existence:
all sentient beings originally perceive existence;
it is only later, upon encountering false teachers, that they give rise to the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, among the four propositions, there is this first one:
the initial prose section establishes that things possessing an intrinsic nature arise through the conjunction of conditions;
whereas if they lacked an intrinsic nature, they would ultimately never arise, even with the conjunction of conditions.
In the response, the first half restates the general negation,
clarifying that the two meanings of "various conditions" and "intrinsic nature" are mutually contradictory;
if there were an intrinsic nature, it would not depend upon conditions.
If it depends on conditions, then its intrinsic nature is lost.
To say that it possesses an intrinsic nature yet still depends on various conditions is a contradiction in terms.
The second half refutes this, saying:
"The nature of a jar within the mud is not produced by various conditions.
If it were now to depend on conditions, it would be a conditioned phenomenon."
This is the nature of essential nature (*svabhāva*).
If there were an intrinsic essence, it would not depend on conditions;
if it depends on conditions, then it lacks intrinsic essence.
Question: The second verse of the "Lower Birth" section receives the critique of the Master of the Treatise:
"If intrinsic nature is produced from a multitude of conditions, what fault is there?"
Since all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) of outsiders depend upon the four conditions,
and their nature is itself conditioned,
it too must be produced by various conditions; the first half of the response reiterates this point and refutes it in general.
The second half explains the meaning of the outsiders' doctrine,
clarifying that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not produced by causes and conditions,
just as in the case of those who worship fire.
While it may be produced through the labor of people and various conditions,
who created the nature of fire within the wood?
One should know that this nature has existed from the very beginning and is not produced by various conditions.
If something arises by depending on various conditions, then it is "originally non-existent but now existent," which falls into the fallacy of non-existence in both time periods.
Question: In the second section below, the nature of others (*parabhāva*) is next refuted.
That which possesses intrinsic nature (svabhāva) has the meaning of existing in both time periods;
that which possesses extrinsic nature (parabhāva) has the meaning of not existing in both time periods.
This is because, lacking intrinsic nature, it arises only through dependence upon various conditions.
In relation to self-nature, the manifold conditions are "other" to that very self-nature.
In the first half of the response, the self is used as a metaphor for the other.
The second half explains the refutation.
The intent of the refutation is as follows: that which is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also called "other-nature" (*parabhāva*) in relation to another.
Since intrinsic nature does not exist, other-nature likewise does not exist.
One might expect that "the other" in relation to another is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since there is no intrinsic nature, there is likewise no nature of the other.
At the beginning of the prose section, the intrinsic nature was refuted by means of two arguments.
First, it is refuted by way of the gate of establishment through causes;
next, it is refuted by way of the gate of mutual dependence;
and finally, two further meanings are cited to refute other-nature (*parabhāva*).
For example, a single pillar is composed of four atoms and possesses two types of nominal causes;
therefore, it lacks intrinsic nature.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
Thus, by virtue of its causes, it is empty.
Even if there were a pillar, it would necessarily be long or short;
if it possessed an intrinsic nature, it would not depend upon length.
Because there is shortness due to length,
shortness has no intrinsic nature;
therefore, shortness is empty.
However, there is indeed the distinction between "self" and "other," which must be discussed with precision.
As for those who maintain an interpretation based solely on the first chapter, they say:
That existence exists as something that can exist;
it does not exist by virtue of non-existence.
Since this existence is self-existent, [it follows that]...
Now, that which exists cannot exist [independently];
it exists by virtue of non-existence,
and thus it must be the existence of another.
If it were the case that something exists now due to non-existence, yet does not exist as something else,
then that "other" would not exist by virtue of its own nature because of non-existence;
furthermore, that other would not exist by virtue of non-existence.
Since this is the meaning of "nature," that which now exists by virtue of being previously non-existent is termed the meaning of "provisionality."
Since they are both conventionally established through mutual relation, they should likewise be mutually related as self and other.
Question: Does there exist something external to self and other?
The intent of the previous question was to say that although all phenomena cannot exist through themselves or others,
there must ultimately exist the myriad phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, since you do not allow for the existence of a fixed nature in either self or other,
there must be an existence that is neither caused by itself nor by another.
In the first half of the response, it is clarified that apart from self and other, no further phenomena exist.
The latter half raises the point that self and other encompass all phenomena:
where there is self and other, there are phenomena;
where there is neither self nor other, there are no phenomena.
Regarding the terms "self" and "other," they are discussed in terms of two meanings.
First, as in the case of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the human body's essential nature is considered "self" and the five aggregates are considered "other.
Second, the person within the aggregates is taken as "self."
All phenomena external to one's own [aggregates] are entirely "other.
Thus, the meaning of the categories of self and other exhausts all phenomena.
Furthermore, within the gates of self and other respectively, the inclusion of all phenomena is likewise exhaustive.
As a person is a person by virtue of being oneself,
so a dharma is a dharma by virtue of being itself.
In the world, there is nothing that is not itself.
Since it has been stated that there is no self-nature, there are no dharmas whatsoever.
Furthermore, when things are viewed from the perspective of one another, there is nothing that is not "other.
To refute the "other" is therefore to exhaust all things as well.
The combination of self and other is also exhausted.
The jar is the self;
everything outside the jar is the other.
Question: Below, the fourth section refutes non-existence.
Furthermore, there are three points [to be considered]:
first, the establishment of non-existence by one's own school.
For instance, it is like asserting that conventional truth exists while ultimate truth is definitively non-existent;
in such a case, the proponent, seeking the existence or non-existence [of the ultimate],
instead clings to non-existence.
Third, the proponent first borrows the refutation of existence to refute non-existence;
the opponent then seizes upon this refutation as a proof for establishing [non-existence], and thus clings to the notion of non-existence.
In the response, the first half correctly refutes [the opponent's position],
while the second half explains the refutation:
neither the identity nor the difference of existence and non-existence is established in either case.
If they were of one essence,
then when existence is absent, non-existence would also be absent.
If existence and non-existence were of different essences...
Because there is nothing to be awaited, there is also no non-existence.
Furthermore, since your conception of existence is already false,
your adherence to non-existence likewise arises from arbitrary sentiment.
Therefore, both meanings are untenable.
Furthermore, since you have never existed from the very beginning,
what is it that you claim to be non-existent?
If a person perceives existence and non-existence, one refutes them by combining the second [pair] of existence and non-existence.
There are four ways to refute them separately, and there are likewise four ways to refute them by combining them.
The first verse introduces and rebukes the four errors;
the second verse cites the Buddha’s teaching to exhort the abandonment of existence and non-existence;
and the following two verses further refute non-existence to establish the meaning of such abandonment.
The two verses of the fourth section present the faults of existence and non-existence, explaining the reason for refuting both existence and non-existence.
The long prose states: "If one necessarily seeks a view of existence," this is not a view that exists within either existence or non-existence.
This is precisely because they are deeply attached to all phenomena and insistently seek something to be perceived.

The Buddha is able to extinguish both existence and non-existence. [The following] second passage cites a scripture to exhort the abandonment of existence and non-existence, fearing that an outsider might claim that the Master himself is refuting existence and non-existence.
How can this necessarily be trusted?
Therefore, it is now clarified that because the Buddha personally exhorted one to abandon [it], it should indeed be accepted.
Question: Is this a Hīnayāna sūtra or a Mahāyāna sūtra?
Answer: This is a Hīnayāna sūtra.
The reason for citing a Hīnayāna sūtra is to demonstrate that even within the Hīnayāna sūtras, existence and non-existence are refuted.
How much more so for the Mahāyāna?
Furthermore, if one adheres to existence and non-existence,
not only is one not subsumed within the Mahāyāna, [but one is also excluded from it].
Nor is he one who studies the Hīnayāna;
therefore, he cites a Hīnayāna sūtra.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the attainment of faith by Śreṇika is also cited using the Hīnayāna as an illustration for the Mahāyāna.
If even the Hīnayāna still distinguishes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), how much more so the Mahāyāna?

If phenomena were to possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the following third section—consisting of two verses—repeatedly refutes both existence and non-existence to establish the truth and exhort [the reader] to relinquish [attachment].
If existence were truly real, the Buddha would not urge its abandonment;
since it cannot be found when sought,
yet is falsely claimed to exist, the Buddha urges its abandonment.
The two verses constitute two parts.
The first refutes difference from the perspective of existence;
the second verse refutes difference from the perspectives of both existence and non-existence.
Question: For what reason is the refutation of difference [taught]?
Answer: Deluded people claim that because all internal and external phenomena undergo transformation and change, there exists "existent dharma" (bhāva).
Because existent dharma exists, there likewise exists "non-existent dharma" (abhāva).
Now, since no basis for change can be found, there is no phenomenon (dharma).
Since phenomena do not exist, non-phenomena likewise do not exist.
Furthermore, this refutes the notion of difference.
Some people claim that "arising" (utpāda) means that what was originally non-existent now exists,
while "cessation" (nirodha) means that what already existed returns to non-existence. This would imply that there is no transformation from non-being to being.
If there were change, it would imply non-existence;
since change has now been refuted, both existence and non-existence are fully refuted.
The first half of the second verse reiterates that, as previously stated in the section on "having intrinsic nature," there is no difference.
This first half [of the verse] refutes the doctrines of the non-Buddhist Abhidharma and other systems.

The second half refutes the rumors concerning the *Satyasiddhi* and the Madhyamaka-Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra regarding the distinction between "having causes and conditions" and "lacking intrinsic nature.

If one asserts that things definitely exist, one clings to permanence; thus, the fourth pair of verses below clarifies the faults of existence and non-existence, explaining the subsequent intent of refuting both existence and non-existence.

The reason why the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas refute existence and non-existence is truly because existence and non-existence are the root of all views and the fundamental obstacle to right contemplation;
for this reason, they are refuted.
Furthermore, it is revealed that existence and non-existence entail faults; thus, outsiders are exhorted to abandon both existence and non-existence.

Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not exhort one to abandon that which is free from the faults of existence and non-existence, these [latter] must be abandoned because they constitute such great faults.
The first verse indicates that existence and non-existence constitute annihilationism and eternalism;

the second verse explains how existence and non-existence constitute annihilationism and eternalism. The first half of [the second verse] indicates that existence and non-existence constitute annihilationism and eternalism.
The second half exhorts the relinquishing of the views of annihilationism and eternalism;
these are the root of the fourteen difficult questions and the foundation of the sixty-two views.
Where there is seeing, there is craving.
When craving and seeing are fully present, the fetters and defilements arise once more.
Since afflictions exist, there is consequently karma.
Because there are delusions and karma that cause one to revolve through the six realms of existence, and because of this great fault, the latter half [of the verse] exhorts one to abandon them.
The long commentary states: "As for the mention of the three periods of time, this is the Sarvāstivāda interpretation."
Furthermore, it is said that the effect pre-exists within the cause; this is the tenet of the Sāṃkhyas.
Both the former [internal] and the present [external] fall into the error of eternalism.
To claim that there is no continuity of causes is called nihilism.
The preceding thought serves as the cause and the succeeding thought serves as the effect.
Since the preceding thought has already ceased, there is no subsequent cause;
when the succeeding thought arises as the effect, what is there for it to respond to?
Previously, the views of the Vaiśeṣika and Sāṃkhya were refuted regarding the doctrine of permanence;
now, the views of the two schools concerning nihilism and the doctrines of the Ājīvikas and Ulūka are refuted.
Furthermore, previously, the two schools were refuted individually.
This now comprehensively refutes the doctrine that the cause precedes and the effect follows.
The second verse explains why existence and non-existence constitute the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Generally speaking, there are two types of annihilationism and eternalism.
There are two types of views regarding annihilationism and eternalism:

one concerns phenomena (*dharma*), and the other concerns persons (*pudgala*). The view that when the aggregates (*skandha*) cease, the spirit (*ātman*) ceases, is the annihilationism of persons. The view that when the aggregates cease, the spirit persists, is called the eternalism of persons.
Regarding the permanence and annihilation of phenomena (*dharma*): for example, the Sarvāstivāda school asserts that phenomena are permanent because they exist throughout the three periods of time;
conversely, the view that phenomena do not exist in two of those periods constitutes the doctrine of annihilation.
In short, both are crude speculations regarding annihilationism and eternalism.
Question: In what sense are existence and non-existence considered annihilationism and eternalism?
Answer: For now, let us consider this in relation to the person (*pudgala*).
If a person exists because of the aggregates, they lack an intrinsic nature.
If a person possessed an intrinsic nature that was not established in dependence upon the aggregates,
then the person would persist even when the aggregates were severed and ceased.
Therefore, it is permanent.
A jar and a pillar are likewise;
thus, that which exists is permanent.
However, the continuous succession of cause and effect is called "non-interruption.
Now, if the cause is extinguished and becomes non-existent, then the effect has nothing to succeed to;
therefore, non-existence is itself interruption.
If one looks toward the Mahāyāna through the contemplation of non-attainment,
the mere arising of a mind of existence causes one to fall into eternalism;
yet, the deliberate cultivation of non-thought leads one into nihilism.
Question: Regarding what matters do existence, non-existence, annihilation, and permanence arise?
Answer: One may discuss them in relation to all phenomena;
to grasp their essential tenets is precisely the Way.
If one says that there is a path to be sought, one falls into the realm of existence and this is called the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
If one says that there is no path to be sought, one falls into the realm of non-existence and this is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
As it says in the "Chapter on Formation and Destruction":
If there is any dharma that is grasped, one falls into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
Chapter Sixteen: Bondage and Liberation (End of Section Seven). This single chapter contains both general and specific [teachings] regarding the distance and proximity of birth and existence.
Regarding what is called "the distant":
both the Hinayana and Mahayana, as well as non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) and Buddhists (ādhyātmika), all speak of bondage and liberation.
There are two types of non-Buddhists.
First, it is said that the bondage and liberation of sentient beings occur spontaneously,
without causes or conditions.
All sentient beings will exhaust their cycle of birth and death after eighty thousand kalpas and thereby attain liberation.
It is like a ball of thread wound upon a high mountain: when the thread is exhausted, it stops.
Therefore, there is no need to cultivate the Path to sever bonds and attain liberation.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who say that one must cultivate the path to sever delusions before attaining liberation.
For example, the Sāṃkhyas claim that by knowing the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), one immediately attains liberation.
Those who do not know this do not transcend birth and death.
The Abhidharmikas say there are two kinds of bonds: the bond of the cause and the bond of the fruit.
"Fruit" refers to the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*).
The bondage of the "son" is called affliction (*kleśa*).
There are two types of affliction:
first, bondage by object (*ālambana-bandhana*), and second, bondage by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Now, summarizing the general categories, there are four propositions in total.

First: "conditioned but not bound," which refers to the proclivities (anuśaya) that take untainted objects as their conditions, as well as the nine proclivities that take higher realms as their objects.
The second is bondage without objective referent (*anālambana*),
namely, the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising simultaneously with the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Therefore, they are bound together.
Since they are simultaneous, they cannot serve as mutual objects of cognition.
Thus, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
They do not take themselves as objects, nor are they associated with non-objectification, nor are they co-existent with non-objectification.
The third category consists of those that both take [themselves] as objects and are fetters; these are the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have out-flowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*).
The fourth is neither conditioned by objects nor bound;
this excludes all the aforementioned categories. The *Tattvasiddhi* states:
There are no two types of bondage.
Because mental factors do not arise simultaneously, there is no bondage of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Furthermore, when afflictions take an object as their condition, they do not bind that object.
Therefore, there is no bondage by way of an object.
Those who follow the Sāṃkhya school say:
"When a mind of greed takes a wall as its object, it then becomes bound to that wall."
If consciousness were to cognize a wall, the wall should possess consciousness.
However, it is only when afflictions are established as being deluded regarding objects and obstructing wisdom, thereby binding sentient beings, that they are called "bonds.
Thus say the followers of the Mahāyāna.
The two kinds of birth and death are called the "bondage of the fruit," while the afflictions of the five abodes are called the "bondage of the seed.
The Mahāyāna masters of the northern regions also establish this principle.
Furthermore, there is the teaching of two obstacles:
the afflictions of the four abodes are called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
which are abandoned by those of the Two Vehicles.
If the dwelling place of ignorance is called the obstruction to knowledge,
the bodhisattva eliminates it.
As for what is called "liberation":
Those who follow the Abhidharma see that one attains the Way through existence, whereby the understanding of existence cuts off delusions.
Those who follow the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) see that one becomes a sage through emptiness, whereby the understanding of emptiness cuts off delusions.
The Mahāyāna’s cutting off of delusions is likewise like the *Tattvasiddhi*: it employs the understanding of emptiness to cut them off.

Question: Why does the Abhidharma clarify that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the *Tattvasiddhi* explains that ordinary persons do not sever them but only suppress them?
Answer: Because the Abhidharma maintains that one attains the Path through insight (*darśana*).
The non-Buddhists also perceive existence;
therefore, they sever the afflictions.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, one perceives emptiness and thereby attains the Way.
Externally, one does not perceive emptiness;
therefore, [the afflictions] are merely suppressed but not severed.
Now, when seeking such [a state], neither internal nor external bondage or liberation can be found at all.
Therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on Refuting Bondage and Liberation.
Question: Why is there neither this bondage nor liberation?
Answer: The external opponent's formulation of the meanings of bondage and liberation is in every respect untenable.
Therefore, it is because one cannot find it when seeking it.
Furthermore, to perceive the existence of bondage and liberation is itself called "bondage";
to examine and find that bondage and liberation have no source is what is called "liberation."

Furthermore, although those of the inner and outer vehicles, as well as those of the Great and Small Vehicles, have removed their bonds and are no longer bound by them, they have not yet removed their attachments and remain bound by those very attachments.
This is like being freed from an iron chain but still wearing a golden one.
The Master of the Treatise now wishes to cause them to fully abandon both bondage and liberation; therefore, he refutes [the notion of] bondage and liberation.

Furthermore, those of the inner and outer vehicles, as well as those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, all claim that regarding both bondage and liberation, they seek to sever bondage while cultivating liberation.
Now, I wish to cause them to realize that bondage is itself liberation; because one knows that bondage and liberation are non-dual, one shatters both bondage and liberation.
Furthermore, all the profound and essential contemplations of the Mahāyāna sūtras clarify that there is neither bondage nor liberation.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"Neither bound nor liberated constitutes the Great Ornament.
And as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
The *Vibhāṣā* does not resolve these afflictions.
Now, wishing to explain such sūtras as these, I clarify the contemplation of bondage and liberation.
Question: If there is neither bondage nor liberation, how can this be called the "Great Ornament"?
Answer: To have bondage and liberation is to hold the view of existence (*bhavadr̥ṣṭi*), and thus it is not sublime.
Now, because one is free from all such views, this is exquisite adornment.
Furthermore, to hold that there is bondage which can be removed is the view of non-existence (*vibhavadr̥ṣṭi*).
To hold that there is liberation to be attained is the view of existence;
to hold that there is existence or non-existence is to fall into the extremes of eternalism or nihilism, which is called "ugliness.
To be free from these is the sublime adornment of wondrous contemplation.
Regarding the "near-arising" mentioned in this chapter:
the preceding section clarified that there is neither existence nor non-existence.
An opponent says:
Ordinary persons have bondage but no liberation;
noble ones have liberation but no bondage.
How can you say that neither existence nor non-existence exists?
Furthermore, if one gives rise to views of existence or non-existence, it is called bondage;
to be free from existence and non-existence is the Middle Way and right contemplation, which is termed liberation.
Since the views of existence and non-existence have ceased, yet the attachments regarding bondage and liberation still arise,
the next section is the "Chapter on Bondage and Liberation.
This chapter consists of two parts.
First, breaking the bonds to liberate the root;
second, correctly breaking the bonds to liberate.
Within the breaking of the root, there are two parts.
The preceding section on "Breaking the Bonds" was followed by this section on "Breaking the Root.
Sentient beings and the five aggregates constitute the root of the bonds of birth and death;
extinguishing these sentient beings and the five aggregates is termed "breaking the root."
"Fundamental" (ben) refers to the essence (tǐ).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The limits of birth and death are like empty space."
The limit of the nature of sentient beings is also like empty space;
therein there is no coming and going of birth and death, nor is there anyone who attains liberation.
This clarifies that the two fundamental natures are empty.
This is the great essence of the Bodhisattva’s correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Within the fundamental destruction of bondage, there are three parts;
first, the refutation of permanence and impermanence.
Second, the refutation of the five aggregates;
third, the refutation of the existence or non-existence of a self.
Question: Birth and death do not lack a fundamental basis entirely; this establishes the root of correct bondage.
Regarding the "root of bondage," the Sūtra states that it refers to sentient beings and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Question: How does this definition differ from the one established above?
The previous response established the existence of a person through the phenomena of standing upright;
now, the coming and going [of a person] are cited as evidence for the existence of a person.
The preceding section directly refuted the person and its phenomena.
Now, because the refutation [of the self] involves no coming or going, there is no dharma of a person (*pudgala*).
Question: For what reason is the dharma of a person established and then the dharma of a person refuted?
Answer: The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
The objects perceived through the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings do not transcend the [duality of] person and phenomena.
Now, by refuting the selfhood of persons and phenomena, one clarifies the two kinds of selflessness;
thus, one attains entry into the first stage and proceeds until the realization of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, followers of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna constantly loathe the cycle of birth and death and seek liberation from it.
Now it is clarified that if one perceives coming and going, one cannot bring that coming and going to rest;
only by awakening to the fact that there is no coming and going within coming and going can one finally bring it to rest.
The answer is: Below this, the second section, "Correctly Refuting Permanence and Impermanence," begins.
From the preceding sections upward, the refutation of the five aggregates and sentient beings has been completed.
Now, assuming for the sake of argument that they do exist, two alternatives are opened to interrogate them.
Question: In the "Chapter on the Refutation of Bondage and Liberation," why is coming and going refuted?
Answer: Because the outsider [opponent] holds that coming and going is itself bondage, the refutation of coming and going is the refutation of bondage.
However, the basis for coming and going does not lie outside of persons and dharmas.
If these two were real, one would necessarily fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism;
if they were eternal, then there would be no transition or succession between celestial beings and humans.
Tranquil and unchanging,
how could there be coming and going?
If it were impermanent, its substance would be exhausted within a single lifetime.
Who, then, comes and goes?
The bhikṣu Śāṭhya reckons that there is a single consciousness that comes and goes through birth and death;
others, such as the followers of Sāṃkhya and those of the Mahāyāna, all say it is impermanence that comes and goes.
Furthermore, non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain that sentient beings are eternal and thus undergo coming and going;
those within our own school (adhyātmika) cling to impermanence and thus [also] maintain coming and going.
Now, this internal and external doctrine is refuted.
Regarding the refutation through the fivefold search in the second verse:
it is precisely because sentient beings are considered the root of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that sentient beings are now specifically refuted;
yet, even so, no sentient being exists.
Who is it that comes and goes?
Furthermore, the deluded claim that the five aggregates are either abandoned or received.
Just as when one receives the aggregates of a human being, one abandons the aggregates of a deva,
sentient beings would be permanent and devoid of taking up or discarding; therefore,
[the text] separately refutes the notion of a "sentient being."
The long passage states that "birth-and-death (saṃsāra), the aggregates (skandha), the elements (dhātu), and the sense-bases (āyatana) have one and the same meaning.
This means they are called "one and the same meaning" because they are both termed birth-and-death and also termed aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Furthermore, they share the single meaning of being the sentient beings themselves.
From the perspective of the refutation [of the self], they are identical in the sense that it cannot be found through the fivefold search.
Just as it cannot be found through the fivefold search within the aggregates (*skandha*),
the same applies to the elements (*dhātu*) and the bases (*āyatana*).
The third is the refutation of having a body or not having a body.
The reason for this refutation is that, as explained above,
