because there are no sentient beings when sought through the fivefold analysis, there is no coming or going.
The opponent says:
The sutras state that sentient beings discard one body and receive another, transmigrating through the six realms.
Why, then, do you say there are no sentient beings who come and go?
Now, even though sentient beings exist, one may reprove them for having a body or not having a body.
The first half [of the verse] says:
"If one abandons a human body and receives a celestial body..."
Then those who come and go would have no body;
it would be like a person leaving an eastern room and entering a western room—the one coming and going would have no rooms.
The second half [of the verse] says:
If there were no body, then there would be no birth and death.
What could come and go?
Furthermore, since there is no body, there is no one who comes and goes.
Because there are the five aggregates (skandhas), there can be sentient beings;
since the five aggregates do not exist, there are no sentient beings.
If there are no sentient beings, there is no coming or going.
If one discards the body of the five aggregates to cause sentient beings to come and go,
one should likewise remove the five fingers and roll up [the hand] to come and go.
Furthermore, the first half [of the verse] refutes the coming and going of a substantial body.
The first half [of this verse] refutes the position that the person is distinct from the aggregates;
the second half refutes the notion of a bodiless coming and going;
and this [verse as a whole] refutes the position that the person is identical to the aggregates.
This refers to the two meanings: that although the five aggregates do not exist, there nevertheless exists a sentient being;
and that the meaning of "one" is that where there is a body composed of the five aggregates, there is a sentient being.
Next, he asks about the internal meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding your statement that one becomes a celestial being from a human body:
does one become a celestial being through the cessation of being human,
or does one become a celestial being without such cessation?
If it were extinguished, there would be no person;
who then would create a celestial body?
In this case, there would be no body capable of coming and going.
If it were not extinguished, the human body would still remain;
how then could it take on the form of a deity?
He did not accept this objection, saying:
The human body possesses two kinds of power.
By the power of actual dharmas (*dharmatā*), the entire body ceases and cannot become a celestial body.
It is by the power of the continuity of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) that a human is transformed into a celestial being.
How can you raise such an objection?
Now, regarding the meaning of the cessation of real dharmas, we ask: does the agent exist within the state of non-continuation and non-cessation, or does it not?
Is the human form still present or not?
"If he is not present, by what means is his human body transformed into a celestial body?
If he is present, since the human body still remains, how can it become a celestial one?
He replied to me, "The human body itself is transformed into a celestial body."

Now I ask: does one first receive a celestial body and only afterwards transition into a human body, or does one first complete the transition into a human body and only afterwards receive a celestial body? If it is the latter—having first completed the transition into a human body—then [one subsequently receives a celestial body].
Why is it necessary to undergo another transformation into a human body?
If one were to transform beforehand, one would no longer possess a human form;
how, then, could one say that one proceeds from a human body to a celestial body?
Question: The Sūtra states that there is Nirvāṇa and the descent [of the Buddha]. This is the second chapter, in which the fundamental [view] is subsequently refuted.
The intent of the question is as follows:
Since the Sūtra teaches that Nirvāṇa extinguishes both persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharma), [how can this be so?]
One should know that there must be the arising of persons and dharmas.
How, then, can it be said above that there are no persons or dharmas coming and going through birth and death?
The intent of the answer is as follows:
Because sentient beings and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally unarisen, there is now nothing to be extinguished.
Because they are fundamentally unarisen, there is no basis for bondage;
because there is now no extinction, there is no basis for liberation.
Because there is no basis for bondage, there is no birth-and-death;
because there is no basis for liberation, there is no nirvāṇa.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
Birth-and-death is not disordered, and nirvana is not quiescent.
Furthermore, just as sentient beings who seek above and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are unapprehendable,
there is thus nothing upon which to discourse regarding their arising and ceasing.
Question: If that is so, the second section below next refutes bondage and liberation, further opening up three distinct points;
previously, there was a general refutation of bondage and liberation.
Next, there is the specific refutation of bondage and liberation, followed by the third section, which concludes that there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Regarding the first, the question is posed: "There should be neither bondage nor liberation, for their fundamental basis cannot be found."
The opponent says:
"Birth and death are the root of bondage, and nirvāṇa is the basis of liberation.
If, as you have refuted above, there is neither birth and death nor nirvāṇa, then there would be no fundamental basis."
Since the fundamental does not exist, there should be neither bondage nor liberation.
If there were no bondage or liberation, then there would be no ordinary beings and no noble ones, and no cause and no fruit.
Yet, since bondage and liberation do indeed exist, one knows that the fundamental is not non-existent.
In the response, the first half refutes the bondage and liberation of phenomena (*dharma*),
while the second half refutes the bondage and liberation of persons (*pudgala*).
The first half states:
If the five aggregates were to abide for even a single moment,
they could be bound or liberated; however, as soon as one intends to bind them,
they have already passed away and ceased.
Liberation is also like this.
If one can abide for even a single thought-moment,
then there is neither the conditioned nor is there bondage or liberation.
The second half clarifies that because sentient beings are ultimately empty, there is nothing to be discussed regarding bondage or liberation.
Furthermore, the second section below provides a specific refutation of bondage and liberation, which is divided into two parts:
first, the refutation of bondage; second, the refutation of liberation.
Regarding the two verses on "Breaking the Bonds":
the former verse clarifies that one is not bound by oneself;
the subsequent verse clarifies that one is not bound by another.
All who are bound do not exist apart from self and other.
Furthermore, the first verse clarifies that phenomena (*dharma*) are without bondage;
the subsequent verse clarifies that persons (*pudgala*) are without bondage.
Generally speaking, all discussions regarding bondage do not go beyond persons and phenomena (*pudgala* and *dharma*).
The first verse clarifies that there is no bondage resulting from an effect;
the subsequent verse distinguishes that there is no bondage resulting from a cause.
All that is bound does not transcend cause and effect.
The first verse is divided into three parts.
If the body is what is called "bondage," [then...]
If it is said that "this body of the five aggregates is bondage," this restates the opponent's position.
"When there is a body, one is not bound" is the second part, which correctly refutes the bondage of having a body.
There are four reasons why it cannot be bound:
first, the body does not bind itself,
just as a finger cannot touch itself.
Second, if it were that which binds, there would be nothing to be bound.
Third, if it were that which is bound, there would be no binder.
Fourth, if there were both a binder and something to be bound, there would necessarily be two bodies composed of the five aggregates.
Next, where there is no self (anātman), there can be neither the binder nor the bound.
The second line concludes the rebuke of the opponent.
If there were something to be bound, the preceding [analysis] would apply; thus, the second verse subsequently refutes the bondage of others.
The reason for this refutation is as follows:
it was previously clarified that whether one possesses a self or is without a self, in both cases there is no bondage.
Now, the opponent offers this defense:
Because there is a body, there is bondage through discourse.
However, the meaning of bondage is twofold:
first, the five aggregates (skandhas) are the binder, and sentient beings are the bound.
Second, within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the afflictions are the binder and the five aggregates are the bound; thus,
there exists that which binds and that which is bound,
and one does not fall into the error of [asserting] two distinct bodies.
Leave the upper half loose.
If there is something that can be bound, there must be a separate binder capable of binding it;
one should bring that binder to bind what is to be bound.
If there were five aggregates existing separately prior to the sentient being,
those five aggregates should have come to bind the sentient being;
however, there are no separate five aggregates existing prior to the sentient being.
How do the five aggregates bind sentient beings?
The reason for this refutation is precisely to state that the combination of the five aggregates constitutes a sentient being.
There has never been a sentient being who did not already possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) prior [to birth].
How, then, could the five aggregates bind sentient beings?
Furthermore, "sentient being" is a collective designation for the five aggregates.
If one considers sentient beings, there are no separate five aggregates that can bind them.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Name-and-form bind sentient beings; sentient beings bind name-and-form."
That name-and-form (nāmarūpa) constitutes sentient beings means that name-and-form binds sentient beings;
that sentient beings govern name-and-form means that sentient beings bind name-and-form.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also says:
Name-and-form binds sentient beings, and sentient beings bind name-and-form.
This very bondage of sentient beings is itself the liberation of sentient beings;
it is like a knot in a rope—the untying of the knot is nothing other than the rope itself.
One must not say that there is a separate name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that binds sentient beings, nor must one say that there are separate sentient beings who undergo the bondage of name-and-form.
Question: If it is possible [to say neither], then what is possible?
It correctly breaks the person’s bondage to phenomena;
it correctly breaks phenomena’s bondage to the person.
Answer: It breaks both universally.

The preceding section refuted the notion that there is a person who acts as both the binder and the bound. Since it was stated above that within the body of the five aggregates, there cannot exist a single person who is both the binder and the bound— because one person cannot possess two bodies—
it is now intended to clarify that the person is the binder and the body is the bound.
Thus, there would be the subject and the object;
for this reason, it is now said that prior to the five aggregates being bound, there is no person.
"Who binds the five aggregates?
The text is precisely thus.
Furthermore, there are no afflictions distinct from the five aggregates prior to them.
How can it be said that the afflictions bind the five aggregates?

The long passage states: "If one were to claim that there is a sentient being existing apart from the five aggregates, this would refute the Vātsīputrīya heretics' doctrine of a conventionally existent substantial entity."
It shatters the bonds of affliction and destroys the five aggregates, as well as the tenets of the Abhidharmikas.
First, it refutes the schools that maintain a self; subsequently, it refutes the schools that maintain non-self.
Those who calculate [theories of] bondage and liberation do not go beyond these two.
Question: The Abhidharmika says that when the mind of the saṃskāra-skandha gives rise to afflictions, it binds the other five skandhas.
How can you say that there are no afflictions apart from the five skandhas?
Answer: [As follows:]...
He clarifies that the four aggregates arise simultaneously.
When there is that which can bind, there is no separate pure five aggregates that could be bound.
When there are wholesome or indeterminate five aggregates, there is no afflictive aggregate that can act as the binder.
Furthermore, when the aggregates (skandhas) are defiled, there is no need for further bondage;
when the aggregates are pure, no defilement comes to bind them.
Moreover, the afflictions (kleśas) themselves are the defilements of the aggregates.
When the aggregates (skandhas) are defiled, their essence is not bound by itself;
when the aggregates are pure, no defilement comes to bind them.
How, then, can one speak of a binder and that which is bound?
Furthermore, there is also no second refutation that resolves [the opponent's position].
This is divided into two parts.
The first verse refutes the notion of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
The second verse refutes the interpretation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The initial refutation of the interpretation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the refutation of the meaning of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*);
the second refutation of the interpretation of the unconditioned is the refutation of the meaning of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
This also refers to the meaning of breaking through conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation;
all forms of liberation do not transcend these two.
Question: What is the difference between nirvāṇa and liberation?
Answer: Nirvāṇa is necessarily liberation, but liberation is not necessarily nirvāṇa.
For example, there is conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation.
Therefore, liberation pertains to both realms;
nirvāṇa, however, is exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is the principle common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Within the liberation that breaks conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), there is precisely the opening of the three temporal gates regarding the breaking of bonds.
First, "that which is already bound has no liberation.
This refers to the meaning of severing afflictions (*kleśa*) as treated in this treatise.
For one who has already been bound, the delusion has already ceased;
what, then, is there to be severed?
Furthermore, once the binding has ceased, there is no longer bondage.
If there is no bondage, how can there be liberation?
Furthermore, while the view of self exists, there can be no understanding of non-self.
In these two cases—whether one is already bound or not yet bound—there is nothing upon which liberation could depend, nor is there any liberation.
This clarifies that since delusion exists in the future, how can it be severed?
If the three—delusion, understanding, and liberation—are simultaneous, they cannot coexist.
For example, the view that conceives of a self is delusion, whereas the mind that lacks such a conception of self is understanding.
When the view of self is arising, there is no understanding of non-self;
when there is understanding of non-self, the delusion of the view of self does not exist.
How, then, could they occur at the same time?
Furthermore, there are three propositions:
first, when there is bondage, there is no liberation;
second, when there is no bondage, there is likewise no liberation.
The simultaneous occurrence of the three bonds and their release is likewise impossible; there is no release while one is bound.
This threefold principle is fully established by the opponent's own position:
at the very moment a delusion first arises, one is precisely bound and not released.
Next, in the path of non-obstruction, delusion and liberation occur simultaneously.
Next, in the path of liberation, there is liberation but no bondage.
These three propositions are refuted by entering the present three gates.
Question: The second section below refutes the liberation that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The question is posed first and the answer follows.
This is a question raised by both the Sāṃkhya school and followers of the Mahāyāna.
Statements such as "nirvāṇa exists primordially" and "the nature of nirvāṇa is pure by nature and pure through expedient means" all represent the intent of the present opponent's question.
One might ask: how is it known that this passage refutes the liberation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The answer established in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "There are those who, practicing the Path, enter nirvāṇa in the present life.
Since it is described as an "entry," one should know that this refers to nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The answer is: Below, it correctly refutes unconditioned nirvāṇa;
if one establishes the meaning of the two types of prajñā, above, it refutes conditioned prajñā.
Now, regarding the refutation of unconditioned *prajñā* by the two masters who explain conditioned *prajñā*,
the masters of the South say:
The understanding of the ten stages is entirely conditioned;
therefore, it is called "conditioned prajñā.
The masters of the *Saṃgraha* say:
If *prajñā* were the wisdom of the true essence (*svabhāva-jñāna*) and thus unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
this would contradict the sūtras.
As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
If this eternal dharma is to be called the Tathāgata,
how could it already be eternal while still within the state of cause?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Prajñā transforms into sarvajñā.
How does it transform eternally?
Furthermore, if the wisdom of the true essence (svabhāvajñāna) is eternal...
Regarding the explanation of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), how is the Samaya clarified?
It is the interpretation of the two schools of Unconditioned Wisdom (*asaṃskṛtaprajñā*);
the first takes the realm of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its application.
The second function among the three qualities (*guṇas*) is *prajñā* (wisdom).
The first half of the verse restates the opponent's position;
the second half refutes it directly.
There are two kinds of grasping (*upādāna*).
First, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called grasping.
Second, the mind of attachment is called grasping.
Because these two types of sensation do not exist at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is said that one does not experience any phenomena.
This person, however, does not experience sensation while experiencing non-sensation;
thus, the absence of sensation itself becomes a form of sensation, which is termed being "bound by sensation."
Furthermore, this person claims that although the mind has nothing it receives, in the end there is something attained.
Where there is attainment, there is inevitably reception;
therefore, one is bound by reception.
In this way, one who has left the state of an ordinary person to become a sage may yet return to being an ordinary person.
This applies equally to birth-and-death and nirvana, as well as to the real and the false.
Furthermore, the third single verse, which does not depart from birth-and-death, summarizes that there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Because birth-and-death is itself nirvana, there is no bondage;
because nirvana is itself birth-and-death, there is no liberation.
Thus, both bonds are simultaneously without bondage or liberation.
The first three phrases correctly present the Buddha’s sūtras;
the subsequent single phrase rebukes the outsider.
Those who are deluded often claim that by severing fetters one attains liberation, and by transcending birth and death one attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the two views of bondage and liberation arise;
as the ignorant take these to be two,
we now clarify that realizing the very essence of birth-and-death is itself nirvana.
Because one does not understand the preceding verse, nirvāṇa is instead turned into saṃsāra.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"If bodhi is not attained, bodhi becomes saṃsāra."
If one attains bodhi, birth-and-death itself becomes bodhi.
Question: How is it that birth-and-death is identical to nirvāṇa?
Answer: To realize that birth-and-death is fundamentally devoid of the four extremes is itself nirvāṇa.
Because both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra are equally characterized by the four absences.
For those who discourse on delusion and awakening,
because the sages have awakened to the fact that saṃsāra is fundamentally characterized by these four absences, saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa.
Ordinary beings claim that because the four negations result in non-negation, nirvana becomes samsara.
(Madhyamaka-śāstra-vṛtti, Fascicle 7, End)
